readings.title: A shared laundry room schedule
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents of an apartment building shared two laundry machines. Weekend arguments grew even though a booking sheet hung beside the door. The main obstacle was reservations visible only inside the room. People made plans at home and discovered a conflict only after carrying clothes downstairs. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a record of machine use and complaints. The building committee compared busy hours with the number of missed or duplicated bookings. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated advance access to the schedule reduced conflicts. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a shared booking view with a paper alternative. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: shared facilities need information before arrival. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in a shared laundry room schedule, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Light in a public reading room
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A new reading room had large windows. Readers praised the daylight but moved away from desks when afternoon sun reached their pages. The main obstacle was glare at the most popular desks. The original drawing showed the room in morning light and missed seasonal changes. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used observations across different times of day. Staff noted occupied seats and asked readers when they moved. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated adjustable shade preserved useful daylight. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced movable blinds and revised desk placement. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: good design responds to changing conditions. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in light in a public reading room, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Finding the lift in a housing block
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A renovated housing block added a lift. New visitors repeatedly climbed stairs because signs from the main entrance pointed elsewhere. The main obstacle was wayfinding based on the old building layout. The lift was visible from one corridor but not from the route used by most visitors. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a walk-through with first-time users. Residents watched guests choose routes without giving them advance directions. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated the first junction caused nearly every error. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced new signs at the entrance and corridor split. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: an improvement is useful only when it can be found. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in finding the lift in a housing block, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Ventilation in a meeting room
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community meeting room felt uncomfortable during crowded events. Opening every window helped briefly but caused noise from the street. The main obstacle was a choice between fresh air and audible discussion. Organizers had no record of occupancy or when conditions became difficult. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a monitored series of ordinary meetings. Building staff recorded room use and consulted qualified specialists about ventilation options. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated a planned airflow setting worked better than sudden changes. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced an occupancy guide and suitable ventilation adjustment. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: comfortable shared spaces require measured choices. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in ventilation in a meeting room, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning housing and public building design often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the neighbourhood building improvement programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关住房与公共建筑设计的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the building design team proposing a small improvement to the neighbourhood building improvement programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the neighbourhood building improvement programme. People have noticed reservations visible only inside the room, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
